text:
Interviewer: This is an interview with Floor Miller by Jackie Smith. It is July 27, 1984 and we are n the porch of her home on Mayfair Road. Could you state you full name please?
Interviewee: Floor Eva Miller.
Interviewer: Where were you born?
Interviewee: I was born in Worms, located on the Rhine River in Germany.
Interviewer: Did you grow up there?
Interviewee: No. After I was two years old, my parents moved to Frankfurt a/Main.
Interviewer: So you don’t have any memories of Worms?
Interviewee: No.
Interviewer: Did you ever visit there later?
Interviewee: Yes I did.
Interviewer: Can you tell me a little bit about it?
Interviewee: When I was there, I knew very little about it. I visited there only for a short time. The reason we lived there is that close to Worms is a little village where my father grew up. You actually had to go to Worms by train in order to catch another means of transportation to this little town.
Interviewer: What is the name of that little town?
Interviewee: Horschheim.
Interviewer: Was your father’s family there for many generations?
Interviewee: Yes, they had lived there for many generations.
Interviewer: Where was your mother from?
Interviewee: My mother had been born in Frankfurt a/Main.
Interviewer: Had her family been there for a long time?
Interviewee: Her parents moved there after they got married. They moved there from another little town in Germany.
Interviewer: Did you have any brothers and sisters?
Interviewee: No, I am an only child.
Interviewer: What sort of professions did your grandfathers have?
Interviewee: My grandfather on my mother’s side, had a butcher shop. He owned a butcher shop. By the way, I never knew him, he died before I was born. My grandmother, on my mother’s side, grew up in the vineyard region near the Rhine River. She did not work outside the house, that was not common at that time. My father’s father lived always in this small town of Horschheim. He did some farming. My grandmother also never worked outside the home.
Interviewer: What sort of education did your parents have?
Interviewee: Of course they graduated from high school. My mother had a few more years of education. I cannot recall the school she went to. She had been in Frankfurt, and in Frankfurt there was a better opportunity to further your education than there was in a village.
Interviewer: What sort of religious education did they have?
Interviewee: They attended synagogue services. For my father that meant and he always talked about it, two hours of hiking to Worms. By the way, in Worms was the oldest active synagogue in Europe. For my mother that was not a problem. In the city of Frankfurt there were several synagogues. Other than that, there was no religious instruction, as we know it now. They grew up and were taught by their parents and they knew the observances and Holy Days, etc.
Interviewer: Were they Orthodox?
Interviewee: I believe you could call them Conservative.
Interviewer: This means that they were a little liberal.
Interviewee: Yes, they were not strictly Orthodox.
Interviewer: Would you say that they were fairly well assimilated?
Interviewee: Oh, absolutely, yes.
Interviewer: Did they have a lot of Gentile friends?
Interviewee: Yes, some very close friends. In Frankfurt, I recall when I grew up, a couple who had a child of my age. That was a non-Jewish couple. They were often together. They associated also with some of our relatives. There were several of these relatives living in Frankfurt with whom we got together.
Interviewer: What kind of religious training did you have? Did you go to synagogue regularly?
Interviewee: I attended a day school. There I, of course, learned Hebrew writing, reading and speaking. Unfortunately, I forgot a lot of it. My father and I, we walked every Friday evening to the synagogue and we attended, of course, together with my mother, the Holy Day services.
Interviewer: Did you have any relatives living in your home with you?
Interviewee: My grandmother lived with us. I shared a room with my grandmother. That was the grandmother on my mother’s side who had been widowed.
Interviewer: Do you recall why you moved from Worms to Frankfurt a/Main?
Interviewee: Yes, it had to do with business establishment. Later, my father’s brother moved to Switzerland with his family. He urged my father to move likewise, because he saw great possibilities there, so we moved to Zurich, Switzerland. I attended school there.
Interviewer: How old were you then?
Interviewee: Approximately six years old.
Interviewer: During the years you lived in Frankfurt your grandmother moved with you and then stayed with you in Switzerland?
Interviewee: Yes, she did.
Interviewer: What kind of a home did you have in Switzerland? Was it in an apartment or a house?
Interviewee: At that time, we lived in an apartment, actually in a very lovely large apartment. I do remember that well. When we moved back to Frankfurt, we lived in a house with a beautiful garden and I did a lot of gardening.
Interviewer: Did you go to school at all in Frankfurt, the first time you lived there?
Interviewee: I went to a Catholic kindergarten. There was no other kindergarten available.
Interviewer: Do you remember if you were the only Jew in your class?
Interviewee: I believe that, for a while, I was the only Jewish girl. That didn’t make any difference at the time.
Interviewer: You felt perfectly accepted?
Interviewee: Oh, yes.
Interviewer: What kind of home did you have in Zurich?
Interviewee: We had a very lovely apartment with a balcony. I even have pictures from that. I recall that we had a fairly formal living room. At that time, it was called a “salon”. It was a room with light furniture and a black piano in it. That impressed me quite a bit. In Switzerland, the school was quite different. Boys and girls went to school together. In wintertime the teachers asked us to bring our sleds to school and we went sleigh riding. Then Santa Claus came and each child had to recite something and we got some goodies.
Interviewer: Was this a public school?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: Again, how many other Jewish children were there?
Interviewee: I don’t believe that there were any.
Interviewer: You also felt perfectly accepted?
Interviewee: Yes, very much so.
Interviewer: You had some Christmas experiences then. What did you think of them?
Interviewee: I guess that at that time already, I was very broadminded. My parents never objected to it, objected to my participation. I mean. I was never in any plays, or anything like that. When it came to gift accepting, I was also participating.
Interviewer: Did your parents celebrate Chanukah?
Interviewee: Oh yes, they did. They had the lighting of the candles and we gave little gifts on the first night. Later on, here in this country, I learned that it is customary to give a little gift every night. That was not done then.
Interviewer: Did you move back to Frankfurt for business reasons again?
Interviewee: Partly. My father had served in the German army
